title: Can a table have more than one primary key (no — only one, but it can be composite)?
shortTitle: Can a table have more than one primary key?

s1_definition.profdef: No. A table can have at most one primary key, because the primary key is the single canonical identity of a row. However, that one primary key can be composite, meaning it is made of two or more columns whose combined values are unique even though no single column is unique on its own. If you need several columns to be independently unique, you use additional unique constraints, not additional primary keys.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India gives each account exactly one official identity — there cannot be two "official" identities, or the ledger would not know which one is the truth. But that single official identity can be made of more than one piece. For a joint-holding record, the identity might be the pair of account number plus holder sequence, so neither alone is unique but together they are. That is still one primary key, just built from two columns. If the bank also wants PAN to be unique, that is a separate unique rule, not a second primary identity.
s1_definition.oneliner: Exactly one primary key per table, but it may be composite (several columns together); extra uniqueness needs unique constraints, not extra primary keys.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No. A table can have at most one primary key, because the primary key is the single canonical identity of a row. However, that one primary key can be composite, meaning it is made of two or more columns whose combined values are unique even though no single column is unique on its own. If you need several columns to be independently unique, you use additional unique constraints, not additional primary keys.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India gives each account exactly one official identity — there cannot be two "official" identities, or the ledger would not know which one is the truth. But that single official identity can be made of more than one piece. For a joint-holding record, the identity might be the pair of account number plus holder sequence, so neither alone is unique but together they are. That is still one primary key, just built from two columns. If the bank also wants PAN to be unique, that is a separate unique rule, not a second primary identity.

**One line to remember:** Exactly one primary key per table, but it may be composite (several columns together); extra uniqueness needs unique constraints, not extra primary keys.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason a table can have only one primary key is conceptual, not arbitrary. The primary key defines the identity of a row — the one handle the database and the rest of the system use to refer to it unambiguously. If a table had two primary keys, there would be two competing notions of identity and the database could not decide which one child tables should reference or which one clusters the data. So the rule is firm: `PRIMARY KEY` can appear once per table.

What confuses people is the difference between "more than one primary key" and "a primary key made of more than one column." The latter is completely normal and is called a composite primary key. You declare it by listing several columns in one `PRIMARY KEY` clause, for example `PRIMARY KEY (account_id, holder_seq)`. The database enforces uniqueness on the combination, so the same account_id can appear many times and the same holder_seq can appear many times, but the pair must be unique. This is the right design for join tables and for detail rows that only make sense in the context of a parent.

A composite primary key is common in two places. First, in a many-to-many junction table, such as a table linking customers to the products they hold, where the natural identity is the pair of customer id and product id. Second, in weak entities that depend on a parent, such as transaction line items identified by the pair of transaction id and line number. In both cases no single column is unique, but the combination is, so the combination is the primary key.

When you genuinely need several independent uniqueness rules, you do not reach for more primary keys; you add unique constraints. A table can have one primary key and as many unique constraints as you like. A senior nuance is that very wide composite primary keys can hurt performance because the primary key is often the clustering key and is copied into every secondary index and every referencing foreign key, so many teams prefer a single surrogate primary key and demote the composite to a unique constraint, keeping the benefits of a narrow stable identity while still enforcing the natural combination. Another nuance is that in ORMs like JPA a composite primary key requires an embedded id class or an id class annotation, which is more ceremony than a single surrogate id, reinforcing why surrogates are popular.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores transaction line items where a single transaction can have many lines, such as a bill payment split across several billers. A line is identified only by which transaction it belongs to plus its line number, and neither is unique alone. This is exactly a composite primary key on the pair of transaction id and line number.

Problem 2 — A junior developer asked whether they could add a second primary key on the amount column to speed up lookups. The answer is no — that would be a second identity, which is not allowed — and the correct tool is an index or a unique constraint. This is exactly the "only one primary key, use other constructs for the rest" rule.

The mini-project creates a transaction_lines table with a composite primary key and shows that the combination is enforced while single columns repeat, and a comment demonstrates adding a unique constraint rather than a second primary key.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql
CREATE TABLE transaction_lines (
    txn_id     VARCHAR(24) NOT NULL,
    line_no    INT         NOT NULL,
    biller     VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    -- ONE composite primary key: neither column unique alone, pair is unique.
    PRIMARY KEY (txn_id, line_no)
);

-- Need another uniqueness rule? Use a UNIQUE constraint, NOT a 2nd primary key.
ALTER TABLE transaction_lines
    ADD CONSTRAINT uq_txn_biller UNIQUE (txn_id, biller);  -- one biller once per txn

INSERT INTO transaction_lines (txn_id, line_no, biller, amount) VALUES
    ('TXN-0001', 1, 'ELECTRICITY', 2500.00),
    ('TXN-0001', 2, 'WATER',       800.00),
    ('TXN-0002', 1, 'ELECTRICITY', 3100.00);  -- same line_no=1 OK (different txn)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/composite-key-demo-1.0.0.jar

# Inspect the single primary key (composite) and the unique constraint
psql -d bankdb -c "\d transaction_lines"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a transaction_lines table whose single primary key is the pair of txn_id and line_no, already holding (TXN-0001,1), (TXN-0001,2), and (TXN-0002,1).

Step 1: The first insert adds (TXN-0003, 1). Even though line_no 1 already exists for other transactions, the pair (TXN-0003, 1) is new, so the composite primary key allows it. The row is added.

Step 2: The second insert tries (TXN-0001, 1), which already exists. The composite primary key checks the combination, finds it present, and rejects the insert. No row is added.

Step 3: Throughout, line_no 1 appears for several transactions and txn_id TXN-0001 appears for several lines, proving that neither column is unique alone — only the combination is.

Step 4: The separate unique constraint on the pair of txn_id and biller is an independent rule enforced alongside the one primary key, demonstrating that extra uniqueness comes from unique constraints, not extra primary keys.

```text
Feb 14,2026 10:50:00 INFO  LineItemDao - Added line TXN-0003#1 GAS
Feb 14,2026 10:50:00 SEVERE LineItemDao - Rejected TXN-0001#1: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "transaction_lines_pkey"
Feb 14,2026 10:50:00 INFO  CompositeKeyDemo - One composite PRIMARY KEY (txn_id,line_no); extra rules are UNIQUE constraints.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  INSERT (txn_id, line_no, biller, amount)
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────── transaction_lines ────────────┐
  │ PRIMARY KEY (txn_id, line_no)  ← ONE key,  │
  │                                  composite │
  │ UNIQUE (txn_id, biller)        ← extra rule│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ├─ (TXN-0003, 1)  pair is new   → INSERT   (line_no=1 repeats, that's fine)
    └─ (TXN-0001, 1)  pair exists   → PK violation → REJECT

  "second primary key on amount"? → NOT ALLOWED → use INDEX or UNIQUE instead
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Composite Primary Key ═══

  ┌─ Rule ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Exactly ONE primary key per table (the row's single identity).   │
  │ It MAY span multiple columns = composite primary key.            │
  │ More uniqueness ⇒ UNIQUE constraints, NOT more primary keys.     │
  │ ORM note: JPA composite PK needs @EmbeddedId or @IdClass.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Entity Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────────┐
  │ transactions                 │ 1    * │ transaction_lines              │
  │ + txn_id PK                  │◆──────→│ + txn_id  ┐                    │
  └──────────────────────────────┘        │ + line_no ┘ composite PK       │
                                           │   biller  (UNIQUE with txn_id) │
                                           │   amount                       │
                                           └────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for addLine():
    Pre:  (txn_id, line_no) pair not already present
    Post: row added IFF pair unique AND (txn_id,biller) unique
    Note: single columns may repeat; only the PAIR is the identity
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, a table cannot have more than one primary key, and the reason is conceptual rather than arbitrary. The primary key is the single canonical identity of a row — the one handle the database and the rest of the system use to refer to it unambiguously. Two primary keys would mean two competing identities, and the database could not decide which one child tables reference or which one clusters the data, so the rule is firm: a primary key may be declared only once per table.

What trips people up is the difference between more than one primary key and a primary key made of more than one column. The second is completely normal and is called a composite primary key: you list several columns in one primary-key clause, and the database enforces uniqueness on the combination. So the same value can repeat in each individual column as long as the combination is unique. This is the right design for many-to-many junction tables, identified by the pair of the two foreign keys, and for weak entities that only make sense inside a parent, such as transaction line items identified by the pair of transaction id and line number.

When you genuinely need several independent uniqueness rules, you do not add more primary keys — you add unique constraints, and a table can have one primary key plus as many unique constraints as you need. The senior nuance is that wide composite primary keys can hurt performance because the primary key is often the clustering key and is copied into every secondary index and every referencing foreign key, so many teams prefer a single narrow surrogate primary key and demote the natural combination to a unique constraint. At the National Bank of India our transaction line items use a composite primary key on transaction id plus line number because a line has no identity outside its transaction, and when someone asked to add a second primary key on the amount column I explained that the correct tool is an index or a unique constraint. The line I always state is exactly one primary key per table, but it may be composite, and any extra uniqueness comes from unique constraints, never from additional primary keys.
